title: Psalm 44: Wake Up, O Lord
summary: The community remembers how God gave their ancestors the land, not by their own sword but by his hand, and confesses that they still trust him rather than their weapons. Then the psalm turns: God has let them be defeated, scattered, and mocked, even though they have not forgotten him or broken his covenant. It ends with a startling cry for God to wake up, rise, and redeem them for the sake of his loving devotion.
story: After the private grief of Psalms 42 and 43, the Korahite collection turns to a national disaster. Psalm 44 is the Psalter's boldest communal lament, and one of the few that insists the people are suffering not because they sinned but while remaining faithful. It sets a question against the whole pattern of blessing and curse in Deuteronomy, where faithfulness brings security and unfaithfulness brings defeat. The psalm takes that covenant seriously enough to hold God to it, and it prepares the reader for the confident Zion songs that follow in Psalms 46 to 48, which answer defeat with God's presence in his city.
historical:
The heading calls the psalm a Maskil of the sons of Korah. Maskil is a term of uncertain meaning, often taken to mean a skillful or instructive song, and the sons of Korah were a Levitical guild of singers descended from the Korah who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16); Numbers 26:11 notes that his sons did not die, and Chronicles lists Korahite singers and gatekeepers at the temple.

No specific event is named, and proposals range widely. Some place the psalm in David's time or in the wars of the divided monarchy, when Israel or Judah lost battles to neighbors. Others think of the Assyrian invasions of the eighth century BC, including Sennacherib's campaign against Judah in 701 BC, when many towns fell. Many see the exile after 587 or 586 BC behind the talk of being scattered among the nations, though a claim of national faithfulness fits that period awkwardly, since the prophets blamed the exile on Judah's sin. Some older critics placed the psalm in the Maccabean era of the second century BC, when faithful Jews died for refusing to abandon the law, but most scholars now think the Psalter was largely complete before then. The psalm's lack of detail has let it be prayed in every later catastrophe.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, military victory was widely read as the verdict of the gods. When a people lost a war, observers assumed either that their god was weak or that he was angry with them. Israel's neighbors taunted defeated peoples in exactly these terms, and the psalm feels that shame: the people have become a byword and a laughingstock, with heads shaken at them (verse 14). Verse 12 draws on the slave market: God has sold his people for nothing, like a merchant who lets goods go at a loss.

Spreading out one's hands (verse 20) was the ordinary posture of prayer, arms raised with palms open. To spread them to a foreign god was to pray to an idol. The image of God sleeping (verse 23) is daring, because neighboring religions did speak of gods who slept or traveled, and Elijah mocked Baal's prophets on exactly that point (1 Kings 18:27). Psalm 121 insists that Israel's keeper neither slumbers nor sleeps. The psalmist knows this, and his cry is not a theological claim but the language of someone who feels abandoned.
literary: The psalm is built in four movements. Verses 1 to 8 are a hymn of remembrance and confidence, alternating between “we” and “I” as if a leader and the congregation spoke in turn. Verses 9 to 16 are the complaint, with a relentless string of “You have” clauses that lay the defeat at God's door. Verses 17 to 22 are a protest of innocence, framed as an oath: if we had forgotten God, would he not have known? Verses 23 to 26 are the petition, with four sharp imperatives: wake up, arise, rise up, redeem. The contrast between verse 3 (“the light of Your face”) and verse 24 (“Why do You hide Your face”) holds the psalm together.

outline.t: What our fathers told us: God gave the land
Present trust: not my bow but You
The complaint: defeat, scattering, and shame
The protest: we have not forgotten You
The cry: wake up and redeem us

doctrines.note: The psalm refuses the easy equation of suffering with sin. It names a suffering that comes “for Your sake” (verse 22), one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of what later readers would call suffering for righteousness.

The people appeal to the covenant they have kept (verse 17) and to God's loving devotion (verse 26). Covenant is a binding relationship with promises on both sides, and the psalm dares to hold God to his side of it.
Israel's prayers could argue with God. The psalm treats God as someone who can be addressed with protest and urgent demands without ceasing to be trusted.

words.note: Berit, covenant. A covenant was a formal, sworn relationship with obligations and promises. The claim in verse 17 is that Israel has not “betrayed Your covenant”, which is why the defeat seems inexplicable within the covenant's own terms.

Ur, to rouse or stir up. It is used for waking from sleep. The psalmist addresses God as if he were asleep, which is the psalm's most daring move, and one that assumes God can be roused by the cry of his people.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love, the loyal love God promises within his covenant. The final appeal is not to Israel's innocence but to God's chesed. Even after claiming faithfulness, the people rest their case on God's character.

christ: Paul quotes verse 22 in Romans 8:36, “for Your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered”, in his great chapter on the love of God. He admits that believers still suffer like this psalm's people, and then declares that nothing can separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus. The psalm's picture of sheep led to slaughter also recalls Isaiah 53:7, applied to Jesus, the truly faithful one who suffered without having forgotten God. In Christ the psalm's riddle is not dissolved, but it is joined: the innocent sufferer is God's own Son, and the cry to “Rise up” is answered in his resurrection.

hard.q: Doesn't the Bible teach that faithfulness brings blessing? How can the people claim they suffer though they are innocent?
hard.a: Deuteronomy does promise blessing for obedience and curses for disobedience, and much of the Old Testament explains Israel's disasters as judgment for sin. But the Bible also includes Job, several psalms, and parts of the prophets, which insist that the pattern is not a mechanical formula. Psalm 44 doesn't claim sinless perfection; it claims the people have not abandoned God for idols. Some interpreters think it reflects a specific moment when a faithful generation suffered for an earlier generation's sins; others see it as a deliberate counterweight to a too-simple reading of Deuteronomy. Either way, the Bible lets this protest stand unanswered in the psalm itself, and the New Testament takes it up as a description of the Christian life.

questions: The psalm begins by remembering what God did long ago. How does remembering God's past faithfulness shape how you pray in a present disaster?
Is it faithful or faithless to say “Wake up, O Lord”? What does it reveal about the relationship between the people and God?
Paul quotes this psalm in Romans 8. How does reading it next to that chapter change what the psalm says about suffering?
